S031.name: Diminished_Thinking
S031.description: Diminished ability to think or concentrate, or indecisiveness.

subtypes.Reduced Concentration: Unable to pay attention or maintain focus on specific activities like conversation, reading, or watching TV.
subtypes.Indecisiveness: Extreme difficulty making even minor daily choices (e.g., menu, clothes) and hesitating to make decisions.
subtypes.Subjective Memory Complaints: Complaining of memory decline, such as forgetting where things were placed, due to reduced focus.
subtypes.Clouded Thinking: Thinking feels foggy, dazed, or not clear.

S071.name: Trauma_Related_Amnesia
S071.description: Inability to remember an important aspect of the traumatic event (typically due to dissociative amnesia and not to other factors like head injury or alcohol).

subtypes.Fragmented Memory: Inability to recall only specific parts of the traumatic event while remembering others.
subtypes.Generalized Amnesia: Inability to recall the majority or the entirety of the traumatic event.

S076.name: Inability_Positive_Emotions
S076.description: Persistent inability to experience positive emotions (e.g., inability to experience happiness, satisfaction, or loving feelings).

subtypes.Anhedonia for Happiness: Unable to feel happiness or joy even when good things happen.
subtypes.Lack of Satisfaction: Unable to experience satisfaction or pride even after achieving something good.
subtypes.Inability to Feel Love: Feeling numb to love or affection towards family or lovers.
subtypes.Emotional Numbness: A state where the mind feels empty and nothing is felt, as if all positive emotions are blocked.

S079.name: Hypervigilance
S079.description: Persistent state of being alert and tense about the surrounding environment.

subtypes.Scanning for Danger: Always scanning the surroundings and being alert to find potential threats or risks.
subtypes.Safety Checking: Repetitively confirming safety, such as checking exit locations or observing people around.
subtypes.Sustained Alertness: Unable to relax tension even in safe environments and maintaining a constant state of alertness.

S080.name: Exaggerated_Startle_Response
S080.description: Exaggerated startle response to minor stimuli.

subtypes.Auditory Startle: Startling excessively and flinching physically at sudden noises.
subtypes.Tactile Startle: Being extremely startled by unexpected physical contact.
subtypes.Visual Startle: Being greatly startled and wary of sudden appearances of people or rapid movements.
subtypes.Slow Recovery: Heart pounding and trembling for a long time after being startled, not calming down easily.

S082.name: Depersonalization_Derealization
S082.description: Altered sense of the reality of one's self or surroundings after a traumatic event.

subtypes.Depersonalization: Feeling detached from one's own body or mental processes, as if being an outside observer.
subtypes.Derealization: The surrounding environment feels unreal, dreamlike, distant, or distorted.
subtypes.Time Distortion: Time feels like it has stopped during the traumatic moment, or is perceived as moving extremely slowly or quickly.

symptom.disease_info: Acute Stress Disorder (ASD) is a trauma- and stressor-related condition that develops within days of exposure to an actual or threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violation, either directly, as a witness, or through learning that it occurred to a close other. It is characterized by a constellation of intrusive memories, negative mood, dissociation, avoidance, and marked arousal that begins within 3 days and lasts up to 1 month after the traumatic event, with associated functional impairment. ASD is distinguished from normal stress reactions by its intensity, breadth of symptoms, and disruption of functioning, and from Posttraumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) primarily by its shorter duration and earlier onset. Individuals with ASD are at elevated risk for later developing PTSD, making early identification and intervention clinically important.

patient.personality: Mirza is a cautious, detail‑oriented retiree who finds comfort in solitary, methodical hobbies and in double‑checking everything to keep his world predictable and safe.
patient.stressor: While on a quiet birdwatching trip with a close friend at a remote lakeside, Mirza witnessed his friend suddenly collapse from what was later determined to be a massive heart attack; despite Mirza’s attempts at CPR and repeated emergency calls, his friend died before help could arrive, leaving Mirza alone with the body for nearly an hour. In the days that followed, his usual grounding routines—carefully assembling model trains, tending heirloom plants, methodically reading scientific articles—no longer gave him the familiar sense of reality or control, and he began to feel as though he were observing his own life from the outside. His wife noticed that he spoke about the world and himself in an oddly distant way and seemed unsure whether things around him were “real,” which frightened him given his normally concrete, empirical outlook. Two weeks after the incident, when these unsettling experiences interfered with his ability to engage in basic daily activities and he became afraid he was “losing his grip on reality” since his friend’s death, his family persuaded him to seek an urgent psychiatric evaluation.
patient.chief_complaint: “Ever since my friend died in front of me, I feel detached from myself and like everything around me isn’t quite real.”

S031.name: Diminished_Thinking
S031.description: Diminished ability to think or concentrate, or indecisiveness.
S031.manifestation: Since it happened, my mind feels like it’s full of static—I'll sit down to read a short research article or even the instructions for a model train and realize I’ve stared at the same paragraph ten times without absorbing a single word, and I can’t even decide something simple like what shirt to wear without freezing up and second‑guessing myself over and over.

S071.name: Trauma_Related_Amnesia
S071.description: Inability to remember an important aspect of the traumatic event (typically due to dissociative amnesia and not to other factors like head injury or alcohol).
S071.manifestation: What scares me is that I can recall the drive out to the lake and the sound of the ambulance siren in the distance, but the actual moment he went down and what I did first is just a blank spot in my memory, like a strip of film has been cut out of the reel and I can’t splice it back in no matter how hard I try to reconstruct it step by step.

S076.name: Inability_Positive_Emotions
S076.description: Persistent inability to experience positive emotions (e.g., inability to experience happiness, satisfaction, or loving feelings).
S076.manifestation: My wife tells me the grandkids were laughing and running around me the other day, and I know in theory that used to light me up, but now it’s like there’s a sheet of glass between me and anything good—birthdays, my plants blooming, even a joke I would normally enjoy all just register as facts without any feeling of warmth or pleasure.

S079.name: Hypervigilance
S079.description: Persistent state of being alert and tense about the surrounding environment.
S079.manifestation: Ever since the lake, I can’t stop scanning everyone around me for signs they might suddenly drop dead too—on the bus, in the grocery store line, even watching my wife breathe in her sleep—and I find myself constantly checking where the exits are and rehearsing in my head what I’d do if someone collapsed, so my body never really unclenches.

S080.name: Exaggerated_Startle_Response
S080.description: Exaggerated startle response to minor stimuli.
S080.manifestation: Now even small things like the kettle whistling or my wife coming into the room a bit quickly make me jerk so violently that my heart pounds, my hands shake, and it takes me several minutes of deep breathing to convince myself I’m not back at the lakeside hearing him fall again.

S082.name: Depersonalization_Derealization
S082.description: Altered sense of the reality of one's self or surroundings after a traumatic event.
S082.manifestation: Most of the time I feel like I’m watching a documentary of my own life instead of living it—I'll see my hands moving the tiny train parts or feel my feet walking down the hallway, but it doesn’t feel like they belong to me, and the house and even my wife’s face can look slightly off, as if I’m walking through a very convincing but somehow fake set rather than my real home.
